title: Undo, dot, registers and visual mode
summary: Undo and redo, repeat edits with dot, pick registers, and edit columns with block visual mode.

steps.title: Undo, redo and the dot command
body: - `u` undoes the last change; `Ctrl+R` redoes. vim keeps a long history (`:earlier 5m` even goes back five minutes).
- `.` (dot) **repeats the last change**. This is vim's superpower: make a change once, then `n.` `n.` `n.` to apply it at each search match.
A change is everything from an operator or insert command until you return to normal mode. So `ciwnew<Esc>` is one change, and `.` replaces the word under the cursor with `new` again.
```text
/old Enter   ciwnew Esc   n .   n .   n .
> **Practise:** open **Labs → Vim & nano trainer** and run this lesson's challenges until the keys come without thinking.

steps.prompt: The line is `a a a a` with the cursor on the first `a`. You type `rb`, then `w.`, then `w.`. What is the line?
steps.explain: `rb` changes one character. Each `w` moves to the next word, and `.` repeats `rb`.

steps.prompt: You pressed `dd` five times and deleted one line too many. Which is the quickest correct fix?
steps.explain: Each `dd` is its own change, so one `u` brings back the last line. `p` would paste it below the cursor, possibly in the wrong place.

steps.title: Registers
body: Every delete and yank goes into a **register**. Name one with `"` before the command:
| Register | Holds |
| `""` (unnamed) | the last delete or yank: what `p` pastes |
| `"0` | the last **yank** (not overwritten by deletes) |
| `"a` ... `"z` | yours: `"ayy` yanks into a; `"Ayy` **appends** to a |
| `"+` | the system clipboard (if vim has `+clipboard`) |
| `"_` | the black hole: `"_dd` deletes without touching any register |
`:reg` shows them all. Classic trap: you yank a line, delete another, then `p` pastes the *deleted* one. Use `"0p` to paste what you yanked.

steps.prompt: Match the keys to the effect.
pairs: copy the line into register a
add the line to the end of register a
paste the last yank, even after deletes
delete the line without saving it anywhere

steps.title: Visual and block visual
body: - `v` selects characters, `V` whole lines. Move to extend, then press an operator: `d`, `y`, `c`, `>`, `~`, or `:` for a command on those lines.
- `Ctrl+V` selects a **rectangle** (a block of columns). Then:
- `I` + text + `Esc` inserts the text at the start of the block on **every** line,
- `A` + text + `Esc` appends after the block,
- `$A` appends at the end of every line, even ragged ones,
- `d` or `x` deletes the column, `c` changes it, `r` + char fills it.
Commenting out five lines of YAML: `Ctrl+V 4j I# Esc`.

steps.prompt: Order the keys that comment out the cursor line and the three lines below it by adding `# ` at the start.
steps.explain: Block visual over 4 lines, Insert, type, Esc: the text appears on every line of the block when you press Esc.

items: delete the first 4 columns of 10 lines
add `,` at the end of every line
move a function by cut and paste
change the middle of a long word

steps.title: Comment out a block, in real Vim
prompt: `~/deploy.sh` must not delete anything until the new cache layout ships. Comment out lines 4 to 6 (the three `rm -rf` lines) by putting `# ` at the start of each. Nothing else may change.
In full-screen Vim you would do it with a block insert: `4G` `Ctrl+V` `2j` `I# ` `Esc`. The same edit from Vim's command line uses a **range**:
:4,6norm I#     run the Normal-mode keys "I# " on lines 4 to 6
:4,6s/^/# /     or substitute the start of each line
Run it with `vim -es -c '...' -c x ~/deploy.sh`. Then prove the script still parses with `bash -n ~/deploy.sh`.

checks.name: lines 4 to 6 are commented out, nothing else changed
checks.fail: `~/deploy.sh` is not right yet (`<` is the goal, `>` is your file). Each of lines 4-6 should start with `# ` (hash and one space).

checks.name: it is still executable
checks.fail: `deploy.sh` lost its execute bit. Vim keeps it when it writes the file in place; did another tool replace the file?

hints: A range goes in front of the command: `4,6`. `:4,6norm I# ` types `I# ` on each of those lines.
Careful with the space after `#`: inside single quotes the shell keeps it. `vim -es -c '4,6norm I# ' -c x ~/deploy.sh`.
steps.explain: Block insert, `:norm` on a range and `:s/^/` all give the same file. Pick by situation: Ctrl+V when you can see the lines, a range when you know the line numbers (from an error or `:set number`), `:g/pattern/norm` when the lines share a pattern.

steps.title: Real keys: comment out a selection
prompt: In the trainer: select the three `location` lines with `V` and `j`, press `:` (Vim fills in `'<,'>`, the selected range) and add `#` at the start of each with `s/^/#/`.
steps.explain: Visual line mode plus `:` gives you a range without counting lines. The same `'<,'>` range works with any Ex command: `:'<,'>norm A;`, `:'<,'>sort`, `:'<,'>!jq .`.

steps.title: Real keys: the dot command
prompt: Add `;` to the end of all four lines: make the change once, then `j.` for each other line.
steps.explain: `.` repeats the last change, including the text you typed in Insert mode. Make a change repeatable once and you get every later copy for one key.
